metadata.note: The Portsmouth - Weldon corridor of the Portsmouth and Roanoke Rail Road (1834-1844), the Seaboard and Roanoke Railroad (1846-1900), the Seaboard Air Line (1900-1967, Portsmouth Subdivision) and the Seaboard Coast Line (1967-1968), plus the S&R/SAL Boykins - Lewiston branch (Roanoke and Tar River RR) and the short-lived Pendleton - Murfreesboro branch. Drawn from research/branches/seaboard_and_roanoke_railroad.txt in the site repo (DanielMConnolly/historical-trains), researched 2026-10-27. Only the report's drawable spans are drawn. Before this layer the map drew no part of this railroad. Features are split per span x operator x geometry piece (Rule 4): pieces sharing an operator share one colour and a label 'Company: Portsmouth – Weldon (piece)'. Gaps deliberately left: 1845 (whole line; operation mentioned undated), 1847-1850 (VA section unproven; NC section torn up 1845-1850), 1862-1865 (Civil War: military trains only), Garysburg - Weldon after 1967 (SCL bridge cut).

not_yet_sourced: [OPEN] Portsmouth and Roanoke, all three pieces: end 1844 is the last confirmed year (Jan 1844); 1845-46 operation mentioned by carolana is undated and its operator unclear.
[ANCHOR] Seaboard and Roanoke 1846 Portsmouth - Boykins: the only proven year before 1851; 1847-1850 unproven.
[OPEN] Seaboard and Roanoke 1851-1861: end is the last confirmed year (annual report to 31 Jan 1861); whether civilian trains ran in early 1862 is unknown.

[OPEN] Seaboard Air Line Boykins - Lewiston 1900-1905: confirmed only to July 1905; freight-only by 1951; passenger end somewhere 1906-1950. Its passenger start is confirmed only from 1896 (1888 likely).
Pendleton - Murfreesboro 1892-1895: whether passengers rode, and who ran trains, not established.
Postwar restart month (Nov 1865 is a floor) and whether Feb-Apr 1866 Weldon trains crossed the river or met a ferry.
Date of SCL's Roanoke River bridge cut at Weldon, and how the 1967-68 Tidewater reached Weldon.
S&R's legal birth date given three ways (4 Sep 1846; 5 Jul 1847; the Feb 1846 act's 'Seaboard and Portsmouth Railroad'); the label is unaffected.
P&R completion into Weldon: June 1837 (carolana) vs 'by late 1836' (marker text); June 1837 used.
Exact SAL consolidation month in 1900 not verified.
headway_min and avg_speed_kmh throughout are estimates from a handful of advertisements, except the 1834 running time and the one 1951 SAL timing.
branches_deliberately_omitted: Weldon - Roanoke Rapids - Norlina: Raleigh & Gaston property, not S&R (separate report).
Georgia, Carolina & Northern: separate SAL-system company, out of scope.
Franklin & Carolina RR: freight only, not S&R.
Union military operation Portsmouth - Suffolk - Blackwater 1862-1865: military supply trains, not public passenger service.
Boykins - Lewiston after 1905 and all post-passenger freight years (NC&V, CSX).

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OpenStreetMap: Portsmouth - Suffolk 17.6 mi against the documented 17 mi (carolana) / SAL MP 17.5. Whole main line Portsmouth - Weldon traced 78.7 mi against the documented 78.6 mi (NC Railroad Commission 1891 via carolana) / 78.8 mi (SAL milepost Weldon SA 78.8). Main-line trace by operator: 76.8 mi SAL, 1.5 mi (untagged). No router straight-line leg. Cut points are the trace vertices nearest Suffolk (17.6 mi from Portsmouth; SAL MP 17.5), Franklin (37.2 mi), Boykins (54.1 mi; SAL MP 54.1) and Garysburg (76.5 mi). The Portsmouth end is drawn to the waterfront terminal at the foot of High Street (the 1838 wharf extension, and the 1866 ads' 'foot of High St.' / the 1894-95 station), with a 0.59 km (0.37 mi) straight connector from the end of surviving OSM track to that point. LATER ALIGNMENT: the trace follows the track that survives in OSM (CSX Portsmouth Subdivision, built on the S&R grade); any 19th-century line changes, yard rearrangements at Portsmouth, Suffolk and Weldon, and the post-1860s Roanoke River bridge are drawn on their later alignment, which is the only one mapped.

segments.note: Portsmouth and Roanoke first section. Horse-drawn cars from July 1834 (not drawn as a separate era, Rule 5); the first locomotive, the John Barnett, arrived 4 Sep 1834 and 'began making two roundtrips a day' (carolana) - steam falls in the same calendar year, so the drawn start stays 1834. The Portsmouth depot (High & Chestnut Sts) was extended to the Elizabeth River wharf in 1838 (virginiaplaces); the geometry ends at the waterfront throughout. Aug 11 1837 head-on collision near Suffolk involved a 'morning passenger train' (Wikipedia). Headway 360 from the two round trips a day of 1834 (carolana); later frequency not sourced. End 1844: the company was sold at foreclosure 7 Oct 1843, but trains were still running in Jan 1844 (carolana: on the night of 6 Jan 1844 Rives, agent of the rival Petersburg RR, tore up track below Margarettsville; 'trains again operated temporarily'). This is the last CONFIRMED year, not a known end - no source dates when this service actually stopped. Do not extend without evidence. Carolana also says the road was 'soon ... back in operations' after spring 1845, undated and without an operator - not drawn.
sources: Segment-level: start 1834 (steam from 4 Sep 1834), two round trips a day and the Jan 1844 last confirmed operation from carolana (Portsmouth & Roanoke); 1838 wharf extension from virginiaplaces; 1837 passenger train from Wikipedia. Headway is the 1834 figure only; avg_speed_kmh from the 1834 running time.

segments.note: Portsmouth and Roanoke staged extension Suffolk - Blackwater (Franklin) - Nottoway - Meherrin - Margarettsville - Blakely's Depot (later Garysburg, where the P&R crossed the Petersburg RR on an overhead bridge). The Nottoway was 'spanned' by July 1835 and the Meherrin bridged 1835, but those dates say the rivers were bridged, not that trains ran; the first confirmed passenger service is April 1836 to Margarettsville and Aug 1836 to Blakely (carolana), so the whole piece is drawn from 1836. 'Trains left each terminal in the morning, arriving at the opposite end in the afternoon' (carolana) = one round trip a day, headway 1440 (estimate). Dec 12 1837 derailment near the Nottoway killed two passengers (Wikipedia). The NC miles (state line - Weldon) were torn up after Rives won title to them in spring 1845 and not rebuilt until 1851. End 1844: the company was sold at foreclosure 7 Oct 1843, but trains were still running in Jan 1844 (carolana: on the night of 6 Jan 1844 Rives, agent of the rival Petersburg RR, tore up track below Margarettsville; 'trains again operated temporarily'). This is the last CONFIRMED year, not a known end - no source dates when this service actually stopped. Do not extend without evidence. Carolana also says the road was 'soon ... back in operations' after spring 1845, undated and without an operator - not drawn.
sources: Segment-level: start 1836 from carolana (service to Margarettsville April 1836, to Blakely Aug 1836); end = last confirmed operation Jan 1844 (carolana). Headway inferred from carolana's description of one train each way a day; headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, NOT sourced.

segments.note: [ANCHOR] Seaboard and Roanoke restart after the Sept 1846 auction to the Virginia Board of Public Works (leased to the town of Portsmouth 1846-47, then the S&R company - one train operator under the S&R name, not split): 'Trains departed for Boykins on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, leaving Portsmouth at 8 a.m. The return trip was scheduled on alternate week days' (carolana). 1846 is the only proven year before 1851: service certainly or probably ran wider both ways, but 1847-1850 is unproven (carolana's 'in 1851 ... the railroad again opened for business' may mean a shutdown during relaying). Drawn Portsmouth - Boykins only. Headway 2880 from tri-weekly service (estimate).

segments.note: Seaboard and Roanoke antebellum service Portsmouth - Weldon after the 17 NC miles were rebuilt (via the NC-chartered Roanoke Railroad, absorbed 22 Feb 1849): 'In 1851, new rolling stock was acquired, and the railroad again opened for business' (carolana); 'full operations resumed' (virginiaplaces). Month not found. Through route Norfolk/Portsmouth (Bay Line steamers) - Weldon - Wilmington & Weldon / Raleigh & Gaston. Mid-span check: Fowler lists Blackwater (Franklin) in the 1858 Dinsmore guide. The S&R annual report of 1 Feb 1861 shows passenger earnings of $94,505 for the year to 31 Jan 1861, so trains ran into Jan 1861; traffic 'fell to almost nothing' under the blockade and Portsmouth was evacuated by the Confederates in May 1862 (csa-railroads). This is the last CONFIRMED year, not a known end - no source dates when this service actually stopped. Do not extend without evidence. Civil War 1862-1865: Union military supply trains Portsmouth - Suffolk (- Blackwater 1863) and a Confederate rump near Weldon were not public passenger service and are not drawn. Headway 720 (estimate, not sourced).

segments.note: Seaboard and Roanoke postwar service, Portsmouth - Franklin from 1865: Norfolk Day Book 27 Nov 1865 advertises passengers leaving Portsmouth Tue/Thu/Sat for the steamer Ella at Franklin, and 30 Dec 1865 'every evening, the train on the Seaboard and Roanoke Railroad brings ...'. Nov 1865 is a floor on the restart, not the restart itself. Through to Weldon from Feb 1866 (see the Franklin - Weldon piece). Mid-span check: Portsmouth, Suffolk, Carrsville and Franklin all carry Fowler's 1875 Official Guide letter. Advertised as the 'Seaboard Air Line' system from 1881 (S&R + Raleigh & Gaston + Raleigh & Augusta Air Line) but the S&R company ran its own trains - a marketing name, not an operator change, so no split; the 1896 and 1898 ads are headed Seaboard Air Line. Portsmouth passenger station (later the Seaboard Coastline Building) built 1894-95. End 1900: consolidated into the Seaboard Air Line Railway (carolana, virginiaplaces); service continued under SAL. Headway 1440 from the one daily-except-Sunday train of 1866; by 1896 at least three trains used Portsmouth (720 or better) - both estimates.

Headway 720 from two trains each way read off fragmentary OCR in the 1951 Guide; one round trip (1440) in the Tidewater years - estimates.

segments.note: Seaboard Air Line Lewiston branch (Roanoke & Tar River, formally merged into SAL only in 1911 - a corporate step that did not change who ran the trains). Confirmed running in the SAL 'Schedule In Effect July 2d, 1905': 'Ar Lewiston N. C. 1:00 pm' (Daily Press, 10 Mar 1906). This is the last CONFIRMED year, not a known end - no source dates when this service actually stopped. Do not extend without evidence. The Feb 1952 Official Guide still prints a Boykins and Lewiston table with no recoverable times and daggers Lewiston and Kelford in its index ('For freight only'), so passenger service ended somewhere 1906-1950. Do not draw the post-passenger freight years (Boykins - Kelford is the North Carolina & Virginia Railroad, freight, from 1987). Headway 1440 (estimate).
